title: Advanced conditionals
tagline: Drop the if, invert the clause, and the same hypothesis suddenly sounds like a policy document.
exam: Reading & Use of English Part 4 — key word transformations (HAD, WERE, SHOULD, BUT, PROVIDED, WHETHER)
Reading & Use of English Part 2 — open cloze
Writing Part 1 — essay: formal hypothesis and concession
Speaking Part 3 — negotiating conditions and compromises
why: At C1, examiners expect more than a bare if: inverted and alternative conditionals are a hallmark of formal writing and are tested directly in Use of English Part 4. They also let you vary how a sentence opens in an essay, instead of starting every hypothesis with the same word.

diagrams.title: Dropping if: the inverted conditional

before.text: If I had known about the delay, I would have left earlier.

after.text: Had I known about the delay, I would have left earlier.

steps: Remove if and invert the auxiliary and the subject: Had I.
The rest of the if-clause and the whole main clause stay exactly as they were.
The same happens with were (present/future unreal) and should (possible future).

formula.ex: Had I known / Were she to resign / Should you need
known the risk / to resign / need help

head: Pattern
Structure
Example
rows: Had we left earlier, we would have caught the train.
Were she to resign, the board would panic.
Should you require further details, contact the office.
But for + noun / Were it not for + noun
But for her quick thinking, the experiment would have failed.
You may leave early, provided that the report is finished.
The match will go ahead whether or not it rains.
Assuming that the figures are correct, the plan is sound.
Leave now, otherwise you'll miss the bus.

use.point: Inversion instead of if, for a formal or literary tone

examples.text: Had I known the venue would change, I would have told everyone.
Were the results to disappoint the board, the director would resign.
Should the fire alarm sound during the exam, remain seated and wait for instructions.

use.point: Negative conditions without if: but for / were it not for

examples.text: But for a last-minute donation, the trip would have been cancelled.
Were it not for her sense of humour, the rehearsals would have been unbearable.
If it weren't for the traffic, we'd already be there.

use.point: Precise conjunctions instead of a plain if

examples.text: You can use the recording studio provided that you book it in advance.
The trek goes ahead whether or not the forecast improves.
examples.note: whether or not = indifferent to the alternative

examples.text: Assuming that the bus arrives on time, we'll reach Cusco by noon.
examples.note: assuming (that) = taking something as a starting point

use.point: Implied conditions: the if-clause is understood, not stated

examples.text: Finish the form today; otherwise your place will be given away.
Save your work now, or else you'll lose everything if the laptop crashes.
examples.note: or else, more spoken than otherwise

watch_out.wrong: If I would have known, I would have called.
watch_out.right: Had I known, I would have called.
watch_out.why: No would in the if-clause; the formal inversion drops if altogether.

watch_out.wrong: Were I to knew the truth, I'd tell you.
watch_out.right: Were I to know the truth, I'd tell you.
watch_out.why: After were … to, use the bare infinitive, not the past tense.

watch_out.wrong: Should you needed help, call me.
watch_out.why: After should, the verb stays in the bare infinitive.

watch_out.wrong: But for you helped me, I would have failed.
watch_out.right: But for your help, I would have failed.
watch_out.why: But for is followed by a noun phrase, never by a clause with a verb.

watch_out.wrong: You can go, provided you will finish the work.
watch_out.right: You can go, provided you finish the work.
watch_out.why: After provided / providing, a present tense already refers to the future.

watch_out.wrong: Whether it rains or not it rains, we're going.
watch_out.right: Whether or not it rains, we're going.
watch_out.why: The verb is not repeated; whether or not already covers both alternatives.

dialogue.title: The scholarship interview
dialogue.context: Mateo has a scholarship interview next week, and Miss Vega and Sofia help him rehearse formal conditional sentences.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Right, Mateo — if the panel asks a hypothetical question, don't panic. Use the structures we practised.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Okay... 'If I would be accepted, I would study Engineering'?

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Careful — no would in the if-clause. Try it again, more formally this time.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Were I to be accepted, I would study Engineering at university.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Much better. Now imagine they ask about a mistake in your application.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Had I noticed the deadline earlier, I would have submitted the essay in English, not Spanish.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Good. And if they want to test your judgement under pressure?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Should the scholarship require community service, I would happily volunteer at the library.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Nice. What about persuading them you're serious, even without the money?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: But for the cost, I would already be enrolled — the scholarship simply makes it possible sooner.

lines.speaker: Miss Vega
lines.text: Excellent. Should they say no, what would you do?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: I'll apply again next year — otherwise I'll never know if I was good enough.

items.sentence: ___ I known about the traffic, I would have left an hour earlier.
items.why: Had + subject + past participle replaces If + past perfect in formal, inverted style.

items.sentence: ___ you require further information, please contact the office.
items.why: Should-inversion makes a polite, formal condition — common in official letters.

items.sentence: ___ she be offered the role, she would need to relocate immediately.
items.why: Were-inversion is the formal alternative to If + were, for present/future unreal conditions.

items.sentence: ___ his calm advice, the negotiations would have collapsed completely.
items.why: But for + noun phrase means 'if it hadn't been for'; it cannot be followed by a clause.

items.sentence: You may borrow the equipment, ___ you return it by Friday.
items.why: Provided (that) introduces a formal positive condition, close in meaning to if/as long as.

items.sentence: Finish the report by five ___ we'll have to reschedule the meeting.
items.why: Otherwise introduces an implied negative condition: if you don't finish, we'll reschedule.

items.sentence: The tournament will go ahead ___ it rains or not.
items.why: Whether … or not expresses indifference to which alternative happens.

practice.instructions: Complete each sentence with one word so that it is grammatically correct.

items.sentence: ___ we left earlier, we wouldn't have missed the opening ceremony.
___ it not for the scholarship, Mateo wouldn't be studying abroad.
___ any problems arise, contact the coordinator immediately.
___ for the volunteers, the festival would never have been ready in time.
You can use the lab after hours, ___ that a teacher is present.
We're going hiking this weekend ___ or not it rains.
Submit the form today; ___ your place will be given to someone else.

practice.instructions: Complete the second sentence so that it has a similar meaning to the first, using the word given. Do not change the word given. Use between two and five words.

items.first: If I had known about the delay, I would have booked an earlier flight.
items.second_end: about the delay, I would have booked an earlier flight.

items.first: If she were to resign unexpectedly, the board would be shocked.
items.second_end: resign unexpectedly, the board would be shocked.

items.first: If you need any help while I'm away, call my assistant.
items.second_end: any help while I'm away, call my assistant.

items.first: If it hadn't been for her quick thinking, the experiment would have failed.
items.second_end: her quick thinking, the experiment would have failed.

items.first: You can join the trip as long as you pay the deposit by Friday.
It doesn't matter if the match is postponed or not — we'll celebrate anyway.
items.second_end: the match is postponed, we'll celebrate anyway.

summary: Formal writing prefers inversion to if: Had I known, Were she to resign, Should you require.
But for and were it not for replace a negative if-clause with a noun phrase.
Provided (that) / providing / on condition that state a formal positive condition; whether or not shows indifference to the alternative.
Otherwise and or else imply a negative condition without stating it.
Use these forms to sound more formal in essays and official writing — not in every sentence.
